name: Deep Purplish Vinaceous
lede: Deep Purplish Vinaceous is a dusty mauve-brown from Ridgway's 1912 chart, one of a dozen "vinaceous" shades built on the Latin word for wine.

sections.title: One wine-colored shade among many
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 plate XLIV gives this hue the name Deep Purplish Vinaceous, hue 69′′′, and the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files the nearest category as "grayish purplish red" in its block 262 [1]. The nearest named colors on file are [[artificial-vermilion]], [[mauve-taupe]] and [[somalis]], at 3.1, 3.9 and 4.3 ΔE [1]. Why he reached for wine specifically, rather than another red fruit or flower, is not explained in our sources [2].

In LCH terms it measures lightness 48, chroma 17, hue 8 degrees, Munsell 9.1RP 4.7/3.7 [1]. Its closest distinct match in the library is [[artificial-vermilion]], about 3.1 CIEDE2000 units away, with [[mauve-taupe]] close behind at 3.9 units; its own near neighbor on the chart, [[faded-rosewood]], sits at 4.5 [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
A match within six CIEDE2000 units covering at least five percent of the canvas turns up in 56 of our 23,781 archive paintings, about 0.24 percent, as photographed [4]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 5 of 1,674 paintings, at 4.7 times the overall rate, and is most loved by Paul Gauguin, in three of his fifty paintings here, twenty-five times his own museums' baseline; it most often plays a mid-tone, in 64 percent of its appearances [4].

The earliest dated match is the same Gandavyuha-sutra manuscript leaf, year 1000, that carries [[faded-rosewood]], nine centuries before Ridgway recorded the name in 1912; early centuries are thin in the archive, so this is a floor, not a first, and a photograph of an aged canvas is a screen color, not a pigment test [4].
